Name: Half My House Lost Power in the Heat: What It Means in Arizona
Post Body:
It is a hot afternoon and suddenly half your house goes dark. The bedrooms have power but the living room and kitchen are dead, or one whole side of the home loses lights and outlets while the rest works fine. The breakers do not look tripped, and it is not a full outage because the neighbors are fine. If half your house lost power in the heat, here is what is usually going on and why it tends to show up when temperatures peak.

This is related to but different from a single breaker tripping. If your problem is one circuit cutting out, our post on whether hot weather can cause your circuit breaker to trip covers that. This one is about losing power to a large chunk of the home at once.

Why Half, and Not All

To understand this, it helps to know how power comes into your home. Most Valley homes get two main "legs" of 120-volt power from the utility, and together they make the 240 volts your big appliances use. Your panel splits the household circuits across those two legs. If one leg loses power or develops a bad connection, everything on that leg goes dark while everything on the other leg keeps running. That is why you lose half the house and not all of it. It is a signature pattern, and it points to specific causes.

The Most Common Reasons This Happens

A loose or failing main connection, made worse by heat. This is the one we see most with the half-the-house pattern. A connection on one of the main legs, at the panel, the meter, or the service connection, has worked loose over years of Arizona heat cycling. When the connection is marginal, summer is when it finally shows up: the heat expands the metal, the high AC load pushes more current through it, and the weak leg drops out. It often comes and goes, working when things are cool and failing when the home is pulling hard in the heat. That intermittent, heat-triggered behavior is a strong clue.

A failed double-pole breaker or a bad main. Sometimes the issue is a specific breaker or the main breaker itself partially failing, cutting power to part of the panel.

A utility-side problem. Occasionally one leg of the service coming from APS or SRP is the issue, not anything inside your home. Part of figuring this out is determining which side of the meter the problem is on, because that decides who fixes it.

An aging panel or service connection. Older panels and service equipment that have baked through decades of Arizona summers are more prone to this kind of connection failure. The heat does not create the problem out of nowhere, it finds the weak point that was already developing.

Why Summer Brings It Out

A connection can be slightly loose for a long time and never cause trouble while loads are light and temperatures are mild. Then July hits. The AC runs nonstop, current through the mains climbs, and the heat expands everything in the panel. That combination is what tips a marginal connection over the edge. So a half-house outage that shows up in the worst heat is not a coincidence, it is the heat and the load exposing a connection that was already on its way out.

Why You Should Not Wait This One Out

A loose connection on a main leg is one of the more serious things that can happen in a residential panel. It generates heat right where the most current flows, and that can lead to scorching, melted insulation, and a fire risk inside the panel or service equipment. The fact that it comes and goes can make it tempting to ignore when the power comes back. Do not. The intermittent stage is the warning. It is much better to find and fix the connection now than to deal with what happens if it fails completely under full summer load.

What to Do

Check whether your breakers are actually tripped, since a tripped double-pole breaker can kill part of the home and is worth a single careful reset. If the breakers are not tripped and half the house is still dead, leave the panel closed and call. Do not open the panel cover or touch the meter or service connections. The mains carry the full incoming power and this is not a place to experiment. Note when it happens, whether it lines up with the hottest part of the day or heavy AC use, and whether it comes back on its own. That timeline helps us track it down quickly.

We'll Trace It to the Source

Finding a half-house power loss means working out which leg dropped, where the bad connection is, and whether it is on your side or the utility's. At The Wire Guy Electric (Arizona ROC 365306), we'll trace it down safely and fix the actual connection or component, not just reset something and hope. If it turns out the panel or service equipment has aged past its useful life, a standard 200-amp like-for-like replacement in the Phoenix metro runs $5,200 to $6,500, and a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel runs $6,400 to $8,750. We will tell you which situation you are actually in.

Name: Why Is My Electric Bill So High in Phoenix This Summer?
Post Body:
Open the utility app, look at the projected bill, feel your stomach drop. It happens all over the Valley right around mid-July. The AC has been running since April, the overnight "lows" are in the 90s, and the number on your SRP or APS account keeps climbing. Before you resign yourself to living in the dark until October, it helps to understand what is actually driving that bill, because several of the causes have real fixes.

One quick note before we start. If the heat is also making your breakers act up, that is a separate problem, and we covered it in why your AC keeps tripping the breaker in Arizona. This post is about the size of the bill itself.

Start With the Big One: Cooling Is Half Your Bill or More

SRP's own guidance is that air conditioning can account for 50% or more of a home's total electric bill during an Arizona summer, and in July and August plenty of Valley homes run closer to two-thirds. That means the fastest savings almost always come from how the house gets cooled, not from unplugging the toaster.

The utility playbook here is worth repeating because it works: set the thermostat at 78 to 80 when you are home and let it drift higher when you are away, since every degree above 80 saves roughly 2 to 3% on cooling. Run the AC fan on auto instead of on, which SRP estimates is worth $15 to $25 a month by itself. Keep filters clean, and consider shade screens on sun-facing windows, which can cut cooling costs by up to 25%.

You Might Be Paying Triple for the Same Kilowatt-Hour

Here is the part most people never look at: on a time-of-use plan, when you use power matters as much as how much you use.

As of summer 2026, SRP's Conserve 6–9 plan charges about 40 cents per kWh during July and August on-peak hours (6 to 9 p.m. weekdays) versus about 13 cents off-peak and under 7 cents super off-peak overnight. APS's popular Saver Choice plans work the same way, with weekday 4 to 7 p.m. power costing roughly three and a half times what the same electricity costs midday. You can see the current numbers on SRP's plan comparison page and APS's service plan page.

That gap is why two identical houses can have wildly different bills. The one that runs its big loads at 6 p.m. pays a premium on every one of those kilowatt-hours.

The pool pump is the classic offender. An older single-speed pump drawing hard for six hours through the afternoon and evening peak is quietly one of the most expensive appliances in the house. Moving it to overnight hours with a proper timer, or upgrading to a variable-speed pump on a dedicated circuit, changes the math immediately.

EV charging at the wrong time erases the savings of driving electric. Charging at 6 p.m. on peak can cost several times what the same charge costs after 9 or 10 p.m. Every modern charger and most vehicles support scheduled charging. If you are still deciding on equipment, we compared the options in Level 1 vs Level 2 EV chargers.

Laundry, dishwasher, and electric water heating can shift too. None of them is huge alone, but stacked on peak hours all summer, they add up.

The Equipment Problems That Quietly Inflate Bills

An AC that is struggling costs more every hour it runs. Dirty condenser coils, a weak capacitor, low refrigerant, or leaky ductwork all force longer run times and higher amp draw for the same cooling. If your system runs constantly, short-cycles, or just never quite catches up, the bill problem is inside the AC, not the wiring. That is HVAC territory, and it is why we point people to our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481) for tune-ups, duct repairs, and honest advice on whether an aging unit is worth another summer. Same family, same no-BS approach, different trade.

A tired pool pump motor draws more than it should. If the pump hums, trips its breaker, or runs hot, it is pulling extra current on every cycle.

Old resistance loads add up. A failing electric water heater element, an ancient spare fridge in a 120-degree garage, or a well pump with a failing start capacitor can each add real money without any visible symptom except the bill.

What an Electrician Can Actually Do About Your Bill

Show you where the power is going. We can install a whole-home energy monitor in your panel that tracks usage circuit by circuit from your phone. Instead of guessing whether it is the AC, the pool, or the garage fridge, you see it in real numbers within a week. For homes fighting a mystery bill, this is the single most useful upgrade we install.

Put your big loads on a schedule. Proper timers for the pool pump and water heater, smart switches for the loads you forget about, and EV charging set up to start when rates drop. The goal is simple: move everything movable out of the peak window.

Make sure the panel itself is healthy. Loose or corroded connections create heat and waste, and an overloaded panel limits your options for adding efficient equipment later. If your panel is original to a decades-old house, it is worth reading the 7 signs you need a panel upgrade.

Quick Wins This Week

Set the thermostat to 78 or above and the fan to auto. Change the filter. Move the pool pump to overnight hours. Schedule EV charging after the peak window. If you are on a time-of-use plan, pre-cool the house a couple of degrees before the peak window starts, then let it coast through the expensive hours. And pull up a year of usage history in your SRP or APS app, because the shape of that graph usually points straight at the culprit.

When to Call Us

Call a licensed electrician if you want circuit-level visibility into your usage, if your pool pump or water heater needs a timer or a new circuit, if you are adding an EV charger and want it wired for off-peak charging, or if your panel is too old or too full to support any of it. A high summer bill in Phoenix is partly the desert tax we all pay, but it should not be a mystery.

Name: Federal Pacific and Zinsco Panels in Arizona: Why Insurers Flag Them
Post Body:
Most people find out one of two ways. Either a home inspector flags the electrical panel during a sale, or an insurance renewal letter shows up asking for photos of the panel and then asking for a lot more than that. Two brand names cause most of this: Federal Pacific Electric (the Stab-Lok panel) and Zinsco, later sold under the GTE-Sylvania name. Both were installed in millions of American homes from the 1950s through the 1980s, which happens to be exactly when huge stretches of Mesa, Tempe, Scottsdale, and central Phoenix were built.

If you own a Valley home from that era and you have never looked at the label on your panel, this post is worth five minutes of your time.

What Went Wrong With These Panels

Federal Pacific Stab-Lok. A breaker has exactly one job: trip and cut the power when a circuit is overloaded or shorted. Federal Pacific breakers, tested independently after a Consumer Product Safety Commission investigation in the early 1980s, failed to trip at rates far beyond anything acceptable, with some test scenarios showing failure rates between 25 and 65 percent. Later testing of thousands of Stab-Lok breakers found roughly one in four defective. Estimates have connected these panels to around 2,800 fires a year nationally. Some Stab-Lok breakers can even fail to cut power when the handle is switched off, which is as dangerous as it sounds. It also came out that FPE had falsified UL testing data, which is why you will not find a serious electrician willing to defend these panels.

Zinsco. Zinsco panels have a different failure mode with the same ending. Their aluminum bus bars corrode, and the breakers can overheat and literally weld themselves to the bus. A breaker fused to the bus can keep feeding a shorted circuit indefinitely, cooking the wiring while everything looks normal from the outside. Zinsco panels also commonly show scorching and melting behind the cover with no outward sign on the breaker handles.

How to Tell What You Have

You do not need to pull the panel cover, and you should not. Look at the label on the door. Federal Pacific panels usually say Federal Pacific Electric, FPE, or Stab-Lok right on the label or inside the door, and the breakers are distinctive skinny units with an orange stripe on many models. Zinsco panels say Zinsco or Sylvania, and the breaker handles often come in colors, red, green, and blue. On a lot of Arizona homes the panel is outside, and forty years of sun may have baked the label into illegibility. If that is your situation, take a photo of the panel with the door open and send it to us, and we can usually identify it on sight.

Why Insurance Companies Care So Much

Insurers have been tightening on electrical risk for years, and FPE and Zinsco panels are at the top of their list. Depending on the carrier, a flagged panel can mean a required replacement before they will write the policy, a non-renewal notice on an existing policy, or an exclusion that leaves you exposed on exactly the kind of fire these panels cause. Inspection-driven states saw this first, but carriers apply the same playbook in Arizona, and we hear from more homeowners every year who got the letter.

It bites during a sale, too. A buyer's inspector will flag the panel, the buyer's insurer may refuse to bind coverage until it is replaced, and suddenly your closing depends on an electrical project you did not plan. If a sale is anywhere on your horizon, we walked through this dynamic in our post on electrical inspections before selling a home in Phoenix.

The Arizona Wrinkle: Heat Makes Old Panels Worse

Most Valley panels live outdoors, often on a west-facing wall that bakes at 115 degrees all afternoon. Decades of daily heating and cooling cycles work connections loose and age breaker internals faster than the same panel would age in a mild climate. A panel design that was already marginal when it was new has had a rough forty years here. This is one reason we take FPE and Zinsco panels more seriously in Arizona than a checklist from a milder state would suggest.

What Replacement Actually Involves (and Costs)

First, what does not work: swapping in replacement breakers. Aftermarket Stab-Lok-style breakers exist, but they do not fix the bus design, the connection points, or anything else structural about the panel. Insurers generally do not accept it either. The fix is a new panel.

A standard 200-amp like-for-like panel replacement in the Phoenix metro runs $5,200 to $6,500. A full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter base and panel runs $6,400 to $8,750. Those numbers include permits and coordination with SRP or APS for the disconnect and reconnect, and you should plan on a day without power while the work happens. We broke down where that money goes in our full guide to electrical panel upgrade costs in Arizona, and you can see what the work looks like on our panel upgrade service page.

The upside is real: a modern panel with room for the way homes actually run now, an insurance file that closes instead of escalating, and one less thing for a future buyer's inspector to find. Most carriers reinstate or bind coverage quickly once you send photos of the new panel and the finaled permit.

Not Sure Whether Yours Needs to Go?

Not every old panel is an emergency, and we are not in the business of scaring people into replacements. If your panel is a flagged brand, though, the honest answer is that it is a question of when, not if. If you are seeing symptoms in the meantime, flickering, warm breakers, or a panel that trips oddly, our post on the 7 signs you need a panel upgrade covers what those symptoms mean.

When to Call Us

Call a licensed electrician if your panel label says Federal Pacific, FPE, Stab-Lok, Zinsco, or Sylvania, if an insurer or inspector has flagged your panel, or if you are buying or selling a Valley home built between the 1950s and the 1980s and nobody has looked at the electrical yet. Send us a photo of the panel and we will tell you straight what you have and whether it needs to go.

At The Wire Guy Electric (Arizona ROC 365306), we replace flagged panels across the Valley, handle the permits and utility coordination, and give you the documentation your insurer wants to see.

Name: Mini-Split Electrical Requirements in Arizona: Breakers, Wiring, and Who Does What
Post Body:
The garage gym that is unusable by 9 a.m. The casita the main AC never reaches. The Arizona room that was never on the duct system in the first place. The back-office bedroom that runs five degrees hotter than the rest of the house. All over the Valley, the answer to these rooms has become the same: a ductless mini-split. And right after people pick one out, the next question shows up: do I need an electrician for this, or does the AC company handle everything?

The short answer is both, and the electrical side is the part that surprises people. Here is what a mini-split actually needs from your electrical system, and who does what on a clean installation.

Yes, It Needs Its Own Circuit

A mini-split is not a window unit you plug into the wall. Nearly every system gets a dedicated circuit from your panel, and most systems 12,000 BTU and up run on 208/230 volts, the same class of power as your dryer or your central AC. Some small 9,000 to 12,000 BTU units come in 115-volt versions, but the majority of what gets installed in Arizona, and anything cooling a garage in July, is 230 volts.

The exact breaker and wire size come off the unit's nameplate, which lists the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP). That nameplate, not a generic chart, is what your electrician sizes to. As a rough guide, though: a 9,000 to 12,000 BTU unit at 230 volts typically wants a 15-amp breaker, an 18,000 BTU unit around 20 amps, a 24,000 BTU unit around 25 amps, and a 36,000 BTU unit around 30 amps, with wire gauge sized to match.

The Parts People Forget

The disconnect. Code requires a shutoff within sight of the outdoor unit, so a tech servicing it can kill the power without walking to your panel. It is a small box on the wall next to the condenser, and it is not optional.

The whip and the right wire. The connection from the disconnect to the unit runs through a weatherproof whip, and the circuit itself has to be the correct gauge for the breaker protecting it. Undersized wire on a compressor load in Arizona heat is exactly how insulation cooks.

Surge protection. Mini-splits are inverter-driven machines, and the control board is the most expensive part in the box. Between monsoon lightning and grid switching, Valley homes see real surges every summer. A whole-house surge protector is cheap insurance for every board in the house, and we covered the details in our whole-house surge protector guide.

Panel capacity. This is the big one. A mini-split is often the third or fourth major load added to a panel that was sized decades ago, right behind the EV charger and the hot tub. Sometimes there is room, sometimes the panel is physically full, and sometimes a load calculation shows the service itself is at its limit. If your panel is older or crowded, read the 7 signs you need a panel upgrade before you fall in love with a unit.

Permits: Yes, Even for a "Small" Unit

Adding a new circuit is permitted electrical work in Valley cities, and the mechanical side of the install is typically permitted too. It protects you at resale and it is not expensive relative to the project. We wrote a full breakdown of when electrical work needs a permit in Phoenix if you want the specifics.

Who Does What: Electrician vs. HVAC Tech

On a properly run mini-split job, the HVAC contractor sizes and mounts the equipment, runs the refrigerant lineset, pulls the vacuum, charges the system, and commissions it. The licensed electrician runs the dedicated circuit, sets the breaker, mounts the disconnect, and makes the final electrical connections. When one crew quietly does the other crew's half, that is where we see undersized breakers, missing disconnects, and circuits daisy-chained off whatever was nearby.

We wire mini-split circuits across the East Valley, often working alongside our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481). Same family, two licensed trades, which means the refrigeration side and the electrical side of your install actually talk to each other. If you are still choosing the unit, their team will size it honestly for the room, and we will make sure your panel is ready for it.

What the Electrical Side Typically Costs

Every house is different, but for most Valley homes the electrical package for a single-zone mini-split, meaning the dedicated circuit, breaker, disconnect, and whip, lands somewhere in the several-hundred-to-low-four-figures range depending on how far the unit sits from the panel and how the wire has to get there. A detached workshop or a full panel changes that conversation, which is why we look before we quote. The one number that matters is the free one: have an electrician confirm your panel can take the load before you buy equipment.

When to Call Us

Call a licensed electrician before you order a mini-split if your panel is more than a couple of decades old, if the destination is a garage, casita, or workshop far from the panel, or if the installer's quote says "electrical by others" and nobody has told you what that means. And call us afterward if an existing mini-split trips its breaker, runs off an extension of another circuit, or has no disconnect at the outdoor unit, because all three are fixable and worth fixing.

Name: No C-Wire? What It Takes to Add a Smart Thermostat in an Arizona Home
Post Body:
You bought the thermostat. You watched the two-minute install video. You pulled the old one off the wall, and there are four wires staring back at you where the instructions clearly show five. Welcome to the C-wire problem, and if your house was built in the Valley much before the mid-2000s, there is a good chance you are about to meet it.

It is one of the most common low-voltage calls we get once the heat sets in, usually from somebody who was told this would be a fifteen-minute Saturday project. Here is what the C-wire actually does, why so many Arizona homes never got one, and the four ways this gets solved.

What the C-Wire Actually Does

The old round mechanical thermostat on your wall did not need power. It was a switch, and a fairly dumb one. It closed a 24-volt circuit when the room got warm and opened it when the room cooled off, and that was the whole job.

A smart thermostat is a small computer. It has a screen, a wifi radio, occupancy and humidity sensors, and it needs steady power twenty-four hours a day whether your AC is running or not. The C-wire, short for common, is what completes that 24-volt circuit back to the transformer at your air handler. It is the return path that lets the thermostat draw continuous power without switching your equipment on.

Without a C-wire, a smart thermostat has to steal its power by trickling a small current through the cooling or heating wire while the system is idle. Manufacturers call it power sharing. It works, sometimes, in mild climates. In a Phoenix summer we see it show up as a buzzing contactor at the condenser, a system that short cycles for no obvious reason, or a thermostat that keeps dropping off wifi and rebooting itself. None of those are things you want to diagnose in August.

Why So Many Valley Homes Do Not Have One

Nobody hid your C-wire. In most cases it was simply never run.

When your house was built, the electrician or the HVAC installer pulled whatever thermostat cable the equipment of that era needed, and four conductors covered it: power, cooling, fan, heat. An extra conductor was extra cost on a tract of two hundred houses, so it got skipped. Multiply that by every subdivision built across Mesa, Gilbert, and Chandler through the eighties and nineties and you have a lot of four-wire walls.

There is a second wrinkle that catches Arizona homeowners specifically. Many Valley homes run heat pumps rather than gas furnaces, and a heat pump needs a conductor for the reversing valve, usually labeled O or B. So you can pull off a thermostat, count five wires, feel good about it, and discover that all five are already spoken for with nothing left over for common. Add a second stage or auxiliary heat strips and the count climbs again.

The Four Ways This Gets Solved

1. There is already a spare wire in the wall. This is the outcome everyone hopes for, and it happens more than you would guess. Installers often pulled a five or six conductor cable, used what they needed, and pushed the extras back into the wall at both ends. If there is an unused conductor sitting behind the thermostat plate and a matching one tucked behind the air handler, it gets landed on C at both ends and you are done. This is a short visit, not a project.

2. An add-a-wire adapter. These are small modules that mount at the air handler and let a four-wire cable carry the signals of five. Some thermostats ship with one in the box. They work, and we install them when the alternative is opening up finished walls, but understand what you are buying: one more component in the chain that can fail, sitting inside your air handler where you will never think to look for it.

3. Run new thermostat cable. This is the permanent answer. A fresh run of eight-conductor cable from the thermostat location to the equipment gives you your C-wire plus spares for whatever you install a decade from now. In a single-story house with a walkable attic, this is usually straightforward. In a two-story, or where the wall drops into a slab, it gets more involved and that is worth knowing before we start rather than after.

4. A separate plug-in transformer at the thermostat. This is our least favorite option and we mention it mostly so you can recognize it. It means a visible cord running to the thermostat, and wired incorrectly it can put two transformers on the same low-voltage system, which is a good way to cook a control board. If somebody proposes this as the first solution rather than the last one, get a second opinion.

Why Battery-Only Is a Bad Bet Here

A few smart thermostats will run on batteries with no C-wire at all, and on paper that solves everything. In practice, the wifi radio is the hungriest thing in the device, and in a house where the AC is cycling from six in the morning until midnight, that radio is working constantly.

Batteries die. They tend to die in the middle of the worst stretch of the year, and if it happens while you are out of town, you lose the one feature you actually bought the thermostat for. We have taken calls from people who found out their thermostat went dark three days into a trip. That is an expensive way to save a wire.

Where the Electrician Stops and the AC Company Starts

Thermostat wiring is low voltage, so this is not the same category of work as a panel or a dedicated circuit. Still, the parts split cleanly.

Getting a new cable from point A to point B through an existing wall, through insulation, around fire blocking, and into a finished space without tearing up drywall is electrician work. So is confirming that whatever is behind the wall is safe to work in, which matters in older homes where the thermostat cable is sharing a stud bay with things it should not be sharing a bay with.

The other end of that wire is a different trade. Landing a conductor on the right terminal at the air handler board, verifying the 24-volt transformer has capacity for the added load, and diagnosing a contactor that is buzzing or a board that is already damaged is refrigeration work. When we find a failing transformer or a scorched control board on a thermostat call, we say so and hand it off. We do that a lot alongside our sister company, The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481), which makes the handoff a phone call instead of another week of waiting.

What It Typically Costs

The honest answer is that it depends almost entirely on which of the four scenarios above you are in, and we cannot tell which one from a phone call.

If there is a spare conductor already in the wall, this is a minor visit and the cost reflects that. An adapter install sits a step above it. A fresh cable run is the real variable: a single-story home with attic access over the thermostat wall is a very different job from a two-story where the run has to come down an interior wall from above. We would rather look first and give you a real number than quote a range that turns out to be wrong once we are on a ladder.

While You Have Somebody Out

Two things worth asking about in the same visit. First, a smart thermostat will start showing you exactly how many hours your system runs, and that number surprises people. If your bills have been climbing, our breakdown of why Phoenix electric bills spike in the summer covers what SRP and APS time-of-use plans do to a house that cools all afternoon.

Second, if part of the reason you are upgrading is one room that never gets comfortable, a thermostat will not fix that. That is a different conversation, and we walked through it in our post on mini-split electrical requirements in Arizona.

When to Call Us

Call us if you have pulled the thermostat off the wall and there is no spare wire behind it, if you have a heat pump and every conductor is already in use, if you have already tried an adapter and the system is short cycling or the thermostat keeps rebooting, or if you would simply rather have a new cable run properly than add a module to a system you do not want to think about again.

Post Summary: Four wires where the instructions show five. What the C-wire does, why most Valley homes never got one, and the four ways this gets solved.

Name: AC Disconnect Boxes in Arizona: The Gray Switch Outside That Fails More Than You Think
Post Body:
Your AC quits on a Tuesday afternoon. The tech shows up, walks around the side of the house, looks at the gray box mounted on the wall next to the condenser, and says the sentence nobody wants to hear in July: I cannot work on this until you get an electrician out here.

That gray box is the disconnect, and it is one of the most overlooked pieces of electrical equipment on an Arizona home. It sits outside, in full sun, on a west-facing wall, for twenty years. Then it fails, and it takes your air conditioning down with it.

What the Disconnect Is and Why It Is There

Code requires a means of shutting off power to your outdoor unit within sight of that unit. The reason is simple and it is not bureaucratic: a technician working on a condenser needs to be able to kill the power himself, confirm it is dead, and know that nobody is going to flip a breaker in the garage while his hands are inside the machine.

So every outdoor condenser in the Valley has one, mounted on the wall a few feet away. Power comes from your panel to the disconnect, and a short weatherproof cable called a whip carries it the rest of the way into the unit.

You will find one of three types out there. The most common is a pull-out disconnect, a plastic handle you grab and pull straight out to break the circuit. Older and heavier-duty installs often use a fused disconnect, which holds two cartridge fuses inside. And some homes have a small breaker-style disconnect with an actual switch. All three do the same job. They just fail differently.

Why They Fail Here Faster Than Almost Anywhere Else

A disconnect in a mild climate can sit untouched for thirty years. Ours do not get that luxury.

Heat and sun. A box on a west-facing stucco wall in Mesa is seeing surface temperatures far above the 115 on your phone. The plastic pull-out handle gets brittle and chalky, the gasket dries out, and the enclosure itself expands and contracts every single day.

Thermal cycling on the connections. This is the real killer. Every time the compressor kicks on, the conductors heat up. Every time it shuts off, they cool. Do that a dozen times a day for two decades and the lugs holding those conductors work themselves loose. A loose connection is a hot connection, and a hot connection is what turns a pull-out into a melted brown lump.

Dust and monsoon moisture. Haboob dust packs into the enclosure and holds humidity against the contacts. Then a storm blows rain sideways into a box whose gasket gave up years ago. We pull covers off disconnects every monsoon season and find corrosion on the blades.

The Signs Yours Is Going

Most disconnects tell you before they quit.

Look for a pull-out handle that has gone brown, chalky, or visibly warped. Look for scorch marks or a black smudge around the slot it seats into. Smell for that sharp hot-plastic odor near the unit when the AC is running. Listen for a buzz or crackle coming from the box rather than the condenser itself.

Also worth a look: a whip with cracked or sun-rotted insulation, a box with a missing or hanging cover, rust running down from the bottom, or wasps and dirt daubers that have built inside the enclosure. All of those are cheap to fix now and expensive to fix after they cause a fault.

The Condenser Is Dead but the Breaker Is Not Tripped

This is the scenario that sends people looking for answers at ten at night, so it deserves its own section.

If your thermostat is calling for cooling, the indoor blower is running, and the outdoor unit is completely silent with no hum and no fan, power is being interrupted somewhere between your panel and that condenser. The disconnect is the most likely place. A burnt pull-out, a blown fuse, or a lug that has finally cooked itself loose will all produce exactly this: no power at the unit, and a breaker in the panel that never tripped because nothing overloaded, the circuit simply opened.

Do not pull the disconnect apart yourself to check. Those lugs are live even with the handle removed, because the line side is still fed from your panel. This is one of the few pieces of residential equipment where the dangerous part remains energized after you have turned it off.

If the breaker is tripping, that is a different problem with a different set of causes, and we covered it in detail in our post on why your AC keeps tripping the breaker in Arizona.

About Blown Fuses in a Fused Disconnect

If your disconnect holds cartridge fuses and one of them is blown, replacing it is the easy part. The question worth asking is why it blew.

Fuses do not wear out on a schedule. They open because something drew more current than they were rated to pass: a compressor starting hard, a failing capacitor, a shorted contactor, a motor pulling locked-rotor amps because the bearings are gone. Swapping in a new fuse and walking away gets you cooling for an afternoon and the same failure a week later.

And if somebody at some point installed a larger fuse to make the problem stop, that is genuinely dangerous. The fuse is sized to protect the wire, not to be convenient. Oversizing it means the wire becomes the thing that fails.

What Replacement Actually Involves

Straight disconnect replacement is not a big job, and that is the good news in the middle of a heat wave. We kill the circuit at the panel, remove the old enclosure, mount a new one rated for outdoor use, land the conductors on clean lugs at the correct torque, and replace the whip if the insulation has gone chalky, which it usually has on anything twenty years old.

For most Valley homes this is a same-visit repair in the low hundreds, and it is the kind of thing worth doing while somebody is already out rather than nursing another season out of a box that is visibly cooking.

Two things sometimes turn it into a larger conversation. If the conductors feeding the disconnect are themselves damaged back toward the panel, that run has to be addressed. And if the breaker feeding it is undersized or the wrong type for the equipment, we fix that at the panel while we are there.

One more worth mentioning: the same monsoon storms that corrode disconnects put surges onto your service, and the compressor and control board on the other end of that whip are the expensive things in the path. Our guide to whole-house surge protection in Arizona covers what that actually protects and what it does not.

Where the Electrician Stops and the AC Company Starts

The split here is clean, which is why the tech in your driveway told you to call somebody else instead of just fixing it.

Everything from your panel to the terminals inside the condenser is electrical: the breaker, the conductors, the disconnect, the whip, and the connections at both ends. Everything past those terminals is refrigeration: the contactor, the capacitor, the compressor, the fan motor, the refrigerant charge.

Plenty of the time both are true at once. A contactor that has been chattering for a year will cook a disconnect, and a disconnect with a loose lug will burn up a contactor. When we open a box and find the damage kept going into the unit, we say so and get the other trade involved, usually our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481). Same family, two licensed trades, one phone call instead of two waits.

When to Call Us

Call us if your outdoor unit is dead and the breaker has not tripped, if the pull-out or the box around it is discolored, warped, or smells hot, if you can hear buzzing or crackling from the disconnect while the system runs, if the cover is missing or the whip insulation is cracked, or if a technician has told you he cannot service your unit until the electrical side is corrected.

And if your system is more than fifteen years old and you have never once looked at that box, walk out and look at it this week. It takes thirty seconds and it is the single easiest way to catch a failure before it happens on the hottest day of the year.

Name: Swapping a Swamp Cooler for Refrigerated AC: What Changes on the Electrical Side
Post Body:
There is a moment every Valley homeowner with an evaporative cooler eventually reaches. Usually it lands in early July, when the dew point climbs and the swamp cooler stops being air conditioning and starts being a very loud humidifier. That is when people start pricing refrigerated air.

Most of the conversation you will have about that switch is about equipment: tons, SEER, package unit versus split system. What tends to get discovered later, sometimes after a deposit is already down, is the electrical side. Going from a swamp cooler to refrigerated AC is one of the largest single load increases you can add to an Arizona house, and your panel gets a vote.

The Load Difference Is Not Close

An evaporative cooler is a fan and a small pump. It runs on 120 volts and typically draws somewhere in the neighborhood of five to eight amps, which is why yours has been living happily on an ordinary circuit for thirty years without anyone thinking about it.

Refrigerated air is a compressor. A three to five ton condenser runs on 240 volts, and depending on the equipment it commonly wants a circuit in the twenty to forty-five amp range. If the system includes electric strip heat in the air handler, that is a second 240-volt circuit that can call for thirty to sixty amps on its own.

The exact numbers come off the equipment nameplate, specifically the minimum circuit ampacity and the maximum overcurrent protection. That plate, not a chart and not a rule of thumb, is what the circuit gets sized to. But the shape of it is always the same: you are replacing a small 120-volt load with one or two substantial 240-volt loads, and that is a real change to your service.

Your Panel Is the First Question, Not the Last

Before anyone talks about equipment, somebody should do a load calculation on your house. That is the math that adds up your service size against everything already connected plus what you are about to add, and it is the difference between an install that goes smoothly and one that stalls halfway through.

Three things we look at on these jobs:

Service size. Most homes that still have a swamp cooler were built when the load expectations were different. If you are on a smaller service and you are adding a compressor and possibly strip heat, that service may not carry it.

Physical space in the panel. Even on an adequate service, you need room for one or two new double-pole breakers. Panels that are already full of tandems and add-ons do not have that room, and stacking more into them is how we end up back at your house for a different reason.

Condition. Some of the panels sitting on these houses are ones nobody should be adding a compressor to regardless of the math. If yours is a brand with a known history, that changes the plan. We covered which ones and why in our post on Federal Pacific and Zinsco panels in Arizona.

If a panel replacement turns out to be part of this, a standard 200-amp like-for-like replacement in the Valley generally runs $5,200 to $6,500. If the meter base has to go with it and you are getting a full service replacement with a new all-in-one meter and panel, that is typically $6,400 to $8,750. We would rather tell you that up front, while you are still planning, than have it surface as a surprise the week your equipment is scheduled. Our breakdown of panel upgrade costs in Arizona goes deeper if you want the full picture.

Worth saying plainly: not every conversion needs a panel. Plenty of houses have the capacity and the space and we simply add the circuits. The point is that somebody should confirm it before you buy equipment, not after.

What Actually Gets Installed

On a typical conversion, the electrical scope looks like this.

A new dedicated 240-volt circuit runs from the panel to the outdoor condenser, sized to the nameplate. A disconnect gets mounted within sight of that unit, because code requires a technician to be able to kill power at the equipment, and a weatherproof whip carries power the last few feet into the machine. If you want the full story on that box and why it matters more here than in most climates, we wrote about AC disconnect boxes in Arizona.

Inside, the air handler or furnace needs its own circuit, and if the system carries electric heat that circuit is considerably larger. Then there is the small stuff that adds up: thermostat cable to the new equipment location, which is frequently not where the old cooler thermostat lived, and power for a condensate pump if the drain cannot run by gravity.

Do Not Leave the Old Cooler Circuit Live

This is the part that gets skipped on budget conversions and it bothers us every time we find it.

When the swamp cooler comes off the roof, its circuit is still there, still energized, now feeding a cut cable end sitting in an attic or terminating at an abandoned roof curb. Sometimes it has been wire-nutted and pushed into a junction box that nobody labeled. Sometimes it is just capped and left.

That circuit should be properly terminated or removed, and the breaker feeding it dealt with. There is also a hole in your roof where the cooler sat, and while patching it is not our trade, it needs to be part of somebody's scope. Ask who is handling it before the crane shows up, not after.

Package Unit on the Roof, or Split System on the Ground

A lot of Valley conversions go with a package unit set on the roof, often on or near the existing cooler opening, because the ductwork is already up there. Others go with a conventional split system: condenser on a pad beside the house, air handler in the attic or a closet.

The electrical implications differ. A package unit generally takes a single 240-volt circuit and needs a disconnect at the unit on the roof, which means the run goes up rather than out, and it means safe roof access for whoever services it later. A split system needs the run out to the pad plus a separate circuit indoors for the air handler.

Neither is automatically better. But the routing, the amount of conductor, and the labor to get power where it needs to go are genuinely different between the two, so if you are getting quotes on both, make sure the electrical scope is quoted on both.

What This Does to Your Bill

Nobody likes this part, so we will be straight about it. Refrigerated air uses substantially more electricity than an evaporative cooler. You are gaining real comfort and real humidity control through monsoon season, and you are trading a low-draw fan for a compressor that runs long cycles in triple-digit heat.

The upside is that you now have something you can actually manage. Once you are on refrigerated air, your SRP or APS rate plan matters much more than it used to, and pre-cooling ahead of on-peak hours becomes a lever that works. Our post on why Phoenix electric bills spike in summer walks through the time-of-use plans and what actually moves the number.

Who Does What

On a clean conversion, the HVAC contractor sizes the system for your house, sets the equipment, handles the ductwork transition from cooler ducting to a proper supply and return system, runs the refrigerant lines, pulls the vacuum, charges it, and commissions it. The licensed electrician handles the load calculation, the panel work if any, the dedicated circuits, the disconnect, and the terminations at both ends.

When one crew quietly absorbs the other crew's half, that is where we find undersized breakers, missing disconnects, and new compressors fed off circuits that were never meant to carry them. We do a fair number of these alongside our sister company, The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481), which means the equipment sizing and the electrical capacity get talked through together instead of discovered separately.

When to Call Us

Call us before you sign anything if your house still has a swamp cooler and you are pricing refrigerated air, especially if your panel is original to the house, if it is already full, or if you have no idea what size service you have. A load calculation early is the cheapest step in this entire project and it is the one that keeps the timeline honest.

Call us during the project if your HVAC quote says electrical by others and nobody has explained what that covers. And call us after, if a conversion was done without a disconnect at the unit, if the old cooler circuit was left live in the attic, or if the new system has been tripping its breaker since the day it went in.

At The Wire Guy Electric (Arizona ROC 365306), we handle the electrical half of swamp cooler conversions the right way: real load math first, correctly sized circuits, a disconnect where code wants it, and the old cooler circuit dealt with properly instead of left hanging.

Post Summary: Swapping an evaporative cooler for refrigerated air is a huge load increase. What your panel has to handle and what actually gets installed.

Name: Casita and ADU Electrical in Arizona: Panel Capacity, Subpanels, and Trenching
Post Body:
You have the plans. Maybe it is a mother-in-law casita off the back patio, maybe it is turning the third garage bay into a rental, maybe it is a 600 square foot backyard unit you have been sketching since the law changed. The builder has given you a number. Then somebody asks the question that stalls the whole thing: is the panel on the house going to carry it?

That question has a real answer, and it is a lot cheaper to get before the slab is poured than after. Here is how the electrical side of an Arizona casita actually works, in the order you will run into it.

Why Everyone in the Valley Is Suddenly Building One

Arizona rewrote the rules. House Bill 2720, the bill most people call the Casita Bill, took effect January 1, 2025 and required every Arizona city over 75,000 residents to allow accessory dwelling units on single-family lots. That covers Phoenix, Mesa, Scottsdale, Chandler, Gilbert, Tempe, and most of the rest of the Valley. House Bill 2928 extended nearly the same framework to counties starting January 1, 2026, which pulled in unincorporated Maricopa County and the smaller towns around us.

So the zoning fight mostly went away. What did not go away is physics. Your house was wired for a house, not for a house plus a second dwelling with its own kitchen, its own laundry, and its own cooling.

Step One: Does Your Existing Service Have Room?

Everything downstream depends on this. A casita is not one more circuit, it is a block of load: a mini-split or heat pump, a range or cooktop, a water heater, a dryer, a dishwasher, lighting, and receptacles that somebody is going to run a space heater and a hair dryer on at the same time.

The way that gets answered is a load calculation, not a guess. We add up the connected load of the house as it sits, add the casita as designed, and compare it against the rating of your service. A few patterns show up over and over in the Valley:

  • Homes from the mid 1990s forward usually have a 200 amp service, and quite often there is real room in it, especially if the house runs gas for the range, dryer, and water heater.
  • Homes from the 1970s and early 1980s frequently have a 100 or 125 amp service with a full panel and no space left. These almost always need the service addressed first.
  • Anything with a panel that is already at capacity, has double-tapped breakers, or is an obsolete brand gets solved at the panel before anybody talks about the casita.

If the service does need to come up, that is a like-for-like 200 amp replacement in most cases, generally $5,200 to $6,500, or $6,400 to $8,750 when the meter base and panel are combined into a new all-in-one and the whole service gets replaced. Our panel upgrade cost breakdown walks through what moves that number, and the panels service page covers what the work involves.

The good news is that this is money you were probably going to spend eventually. A casita just forces the timeline.

Step Two: Sizing the Feed to the Casita

The casita gets its own subpanel. That is not optional and it is not a place to economize, because every circuit inside the unit lands there and everything about the build after that point is downstream of how it was sized.

What drives the size:

  • 60 amps is common for a smaller unit with a mini-split, a kitchenette, a microwave, and no electric range or dryer.
  • 100 amps is the realistic number once you add an electric range or cooktop, an electric water heater, or a washer and dryer. Most full casitas built to be rented land here.
  • 125 amps or more shows up on larger units, or when somebody wants an EV charger at the casita too. If a charger is even a maybe, say so now. Pulling a bigger feeder during the trench costs a fraction of what a second trench costs later.

Size it for what the unit will be in five years, not what is on the plan today. The feeder is the one part of this job nobody wants to redo.

Step Three: The Trench Nobody Budgets For

Here is where casita quotes go sideways. The panel is on one side of the house. The casita is in the back corner of the lot. Between them is 80 feet of yard, and in a Valley backyard that 80 feet usually contains some combination of pavers, a pool, a pool equipment pad, a block wall, irrigation, and a slab patio.

The underground feeder runs in conduit at a required burial depth, and the path matters more than the distance. Straight across dirt is one price. Cutting a pool deck, boring under a driveway, or working around an existing pool and its bonding grid is another, and that is a conversation to have while the landscaping is already torn up rather than after it has been restored.

Two more things worth knowing about the feeder itself. First, long runs need to be sized for voltage drop, not just for amps. A 100 amp feeder that is correct at 40 feet can be undersized at 150 feet, and the symptom is not dramatic, it is lights that dim in the casita every time the AC starts. Second, feeders on a run like this are frequently multi-strand aluminum, which is completely normal and safe modern practice. That is not the same thing as the single strand aluminum branch wiring in some 1960s and 1970s Valley homes, which is the actual hazard people are thinking of.

One Meter or Two?

Most casitas in the Valley run off the existing service on one meter. It is simpler, it is far less expensive, and it works fine when the unit is family, a guest house, or a long term rental where utilities are folded into the rent.

A second meter means a second service, which means coordination with APS or SRP and a much larger scope of work. It only makes sense when you genuinely need the tenant billed separately by the utility. Decide this early, because it changes the design of everything upstream.

What Goes Inside the Casita

Once the subpanel is set, a casita is wired like a small home, and code treats it like a dwelling unit rather than a shed with a bed in it. A typical build includes:

  • A dedicated circuit for the mini-split or heat pump, plus the disconnect at the outdoor unit
  • Two 20 amp small appliance circuits if there is any real kitchen, and a dedicated circuit for the refrigerator
  • A dedicated 240 volt circuit for a range or cooktop, and another for an electric water heater
  • Laundry circuits if there is a washer and dryer
  • GFCI protection at the kitchen, bath, and exterior receptacles, and arc fault protection where required
  • Interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms
  • Interior lighting, exterior lighting at the entry, and at least one exterior receptacle

On the cooling side, most casitas in the Valley end up on a mini-split, and the electrical requirements for those are specific enough that we wrote them up separately in our guide to mini-split electrical requirements in Arizona. If you are still deciding what equipment to put in the unit, our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481) sizes these for casitas regularly, and getting the equipment picked before we rough in the wiring saves everybody a change order.

Garage Conversions Are a Different Animal

Converting a garage is usually the cheapest path to an ADU, and the electrical is usually the messiest part of it.

Garages are typically fed by one or two general purpose circuits that also serve the laundry, the exterior receptacles, and sometimes half the back of the house. The second that space becomes a dwelling unit, that wiring no longer covers it. You need dedicated circuits, correct receptacle spacing, GFCI and arc fault protection, and in most cases a proper subpanel rather than trying to extend what is there.

The other thing we find in garage conversions is existing work somebody did years ago without an electrician: an added receptacle on a lighting circuit, a 240 volt outlet for a compressor, a subpanel fed with the wrong conductors. All of it has to be sorted out before drywall goes up, which is one more reason to have the electrical walked before the framer starts.

When to Bring the Electrician In

Earlier than most people do. The right sequence looks like this:

  1. Before you finalize the design. A load calculation and a look at your panel tells you whether a service upgrade is part of this project. That is a real number and it belongs in the budget from day one.
  2. Before the trench is dug. Feeder size, conduit size, route, and depth all get decided together, and any future EV charger or pool equipment on that side of the yard gets accounted for.
  3. At rough-in, before insulation and drywall. Everything is cheap while the walls are open and expensive after they close.
  4. At trim out, when devices, fixtures, and the subpanel get finished and tested.

The projects that go badly are almost always the ones where the electrical got treated as a finish trade instead of the thing the whole schedule hangs on.

When to Call Us

Call us if you are pricing a casita or ADU and need to know whether your service can carry it, if a builder has told you the panel needs to be upgraded and you want that verified and quoted independently, if you are converting a garage and want the existing wiring evaluated before the work starts, or if you already have a unit going up and need the feeder, subpanel, and interior wiring handled by an electrician rather than a general crew.

We would rather look at your panel for free now than get called out after somebody buried the wrong conduit under a new paver patio.

At The Wire Guy Electric (Arizona ROC 365306), we do this work as a family-owned electrical contractor, which means the person who sizes your feeder is the same outfit that shows up at trim out.

We serve Mesa, Scottsdale, Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe, Queen Creek, Paradise Valley, and Fountain Hills. Request a free estimate and we will tell you exactly what the electrical side of your casita takes.
Post Summary: Arizona's casita laws opened the door. The electrical side is what decides your budget: service capacity, subpanel sizing, and the trench between the two.

Name: Pool Pump Electrical in Arizona: Why It Trips, What Bonding Is, and What Code Requires
Post Body:
The pump goes off and the pool goes green in about four days here. So when a pool pump quits, or keeps tripping a breaker, it turns into an emergency faster than almost anything else in the backyard.

Pool equipment is also the part of a Valley home where electrical corners get cut the most. Equipment pads sit in full sun, they get worked on by pool companies and handymen and previous owners, and the rules that apply to them are stricter than the rules anywhere else on the property. Here is what is actually required, what usually fails, and how to tell which problem you have.

Why Your Pool Pump Keeps Tripping the GFCI

This is the number one call we get on pool equipment, and it is usually one of four things.

Moisture in the motor or the connections. Water gets into the back of the pump motor through a failed seal, or into the wiring compartment through a conduit that was never sealed properly. It does not take much. A GFCI trips on a few milliamps of leakage, so a damp winding will trip it long before you would ever feel anything.

A motor that is on its way out. As windings degrade, they leak current to ground. The classic pattern is a pump that runs fine in the morning and trips once it heats up in the afternoon, then trips sooner and sooner over a few weeks. That is not a breaker problem, that is the motor telling you it is done.

A damaged underground run. The conduit between the panel and the equipment pad gets hit by landscapers, cracked by roots, or filled with water. Wet conductors leak to ground. This one is common on older installs where the run was direct buried without proper conduit.

An actual failing GFCI breaker. They do wear out, especially in an outdoor subpanel that has been baking on a south wall for fifteen years. This is the least likely of the four, and it is also the only one where replacing the breaker is the real fix.

What matters is this: a GFCI on pool equipment is the device standing between a swimmer and a fatal shock. Never, ever have somebody swap it for a standard breaker to make the tripping stop. That is not a repair, it is removing the protection. If yours is tripping, something is leaking current and it needs to be found. Our post on why breakers keep tripping covers the difference between a ground fault and an overload in more detail.

What Bonding Is, and Why It Is Not Grounding

Bonding is the part of pool electrical that almost nobody outside the trade understands, and it is the part that saves lives.

Grounding gives fault current a path back to the panel so a breaker opens. Bonding does something different. It ties every piece of metal in and around the pool together with a heavy copper conductor, minimum 8 gauge solid copper, so that everything sits at the same electrical potential. The pump motor, the heater housing, the ladder and handrails, the light niche, metal fittings, the steel in the pool shell, and the water itself all get tied into one grid.

The reason is simple. If a stray voltage shows up from anywhere, a neighbor's fault, a nicked underground conductor, a failing pump, and the ladder is at a slightly different potential than the water, a swimmer touching both becomes the path between them. That is electric shock drowning. It does not take much voltage, and the first symptom is muscles that will not work, which in a pool is the worst possible symptom.

Bonding is not something a GFCI protects you from. They are two separate systems solving two separate problems, and an older pool can absolutely have one and not the other.

Signs Your Bonding Is Missing or Broken

You cannot see most of the bonding grid, since it is in the deck and the shell. But there are things worth noticing:

  • A tingle when you touch the handrail, the ladder, or the deck edge while wet. Get people out of the water and call somebody. This is not a plumbing quirk, it is the exact symptom bonding exists to prevent.
  • A bare copper wire at the equipment pad that is corroded through, cut, or clearly disconnected from the pump. This wire gets cut constantly during pump replacements and never reconnected.
  • Green or white corrosion on the bonding lug on the motor housing.
  • A new pump, heater, or salt cell installed by someone who left the bonding wire loose in the dirt.

The last one is the single most common defect we find. A pool company swaps a pump in ninety minutes, and the bonding conductor that was attached to the old motor ends up lying next to the pad. The pool works fine. The protection is gone.

What a Correct Equipment Pad Looks Like

A few things are required on every permanently installed pool, and they are easy to check on your own pad:

  • GFCI protection on the pump circuit. Not optional, regardless of voltage.
  • A disconnect within sight of the motor. There has to be a way to kill power to the pump while standing at the pump, and it has to be at least five feet back from the inside edge of the water.
  • Permanent wiring, not a cord and plug. A permanently installed pool pump is supposed to be hard wired in conduit. An extension cord running to a pool pump is a serious hazard, not a temporary shortcut.
  • Correct conduit. Rigid metal or rigid PVC in the right places, sealed, and in good condition. Sun-rotted gray PVC that crumbles when you touch it is one of the most common findings on Valley equipment pads.
  • Receptacle rules. Any receptacle near the pool has to be GFCI protected, and there are minimum distances from the water that govern where one can go at all.
  • A bonding conductor tied to the motor and everything else in the grid.

If your pool was built decades ago, it was legal under the code in effect at the time, and older installations are generally left alone as they sit. The moment equipment gets replaced or the wiring gets modified, though, that new work has to meet current requirements. That is why a pump swap is a good time to have the pad looked at rather than a good time to look away.

Upgrading to a Variable Speed Pump

Most single speed pumps being replaced in the Valley today are going in as variable speed, and there is a real reason beyond efficiency rules: a variable speed pump run at low RPM for longer hours uses dramatically less energy than a single speed pump run at full tilt, often cutting pump energy by half or more. On an APS or SRP summer bill, that is not a rounding error. We broke down where the rest of the summer bill goes in our post on why Phoenix electric bills spike in summer.

From the electrical side, three things change with a variable speed swap:

The drive is electronics, and electronics hate heat and surges. A variable speed pump has a variable frequency drive on top of the motor. That drive is far more sensitive than the old single speed motor it replaced, and it sits outdoors on a pad in Arizona. Shade and proper enclosure ratings matter, and so does surge protection. We cover that in our whole house surge protection guide, and for a pool that is running a drive, a salt system, and automation, it is one of the easier arguments to make.

Voltage matters. Many of these pumps can run on 120 or 240 volts, and they are more efficient at 240. If your existing circuit is 120 volt, converting is often worth doing at the time of the swap rather than later.

The old circuit may not be right anymore. Long runs to a pad at the back of the lot frequently have voltage drop problems that a simple motor tolerated and a drive does not. Undersized conductors on a 100 foot run are something we find constantly.

Pool Heaters, Heat Pumps, and Extra Load

An electric pool heat pump is a serious load, similar to adding a second air conditioner to your house. Before one goes in, somebody needs to confirm the panel can carry it, because the answer on a 1980s Valley home with a full panel is frequently no. That is a load calculation and possibly a panel upgrade, and it is much better to know that before the equipment is sitting in your driveway.

Since pool heat pumps and home heat pumps are close cousins, and since people often end up asking about both in the same summer, our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481) is who we hand the equipment questions to. We handle the circuit, the disconnect, and the panel capacity side of it.

Do Not Troubleshoot This One Yourself

We say some version of this in most posts, and here we mean it more than usual. A pool equipment pad combines water, metal, 240 volts, and conductors that are energized on the line side even when the disconnect is off. Every year people are injured doing exactly what looks like a simple pump swap.

Resetting a GFCI once is fine. Anything past that, including a pump that trips repeatedly, a tingle in the water, or a visibly corroded bonding wire, is a stop and call somebody situation. Our troubleshooting service exists for exactly this kind of find-the-actual-cause work.

When to Call Us

Call us if your pool pump trips the breaker or GFCI, if your pump is dead and the breaker did not trip, if anybody has felt a tingle touching the ladder, rail, or wet deck, if the bonding wire at your equipment pad is cut, corroded, or lying loose, if your conduit or wiring at the pad is sun-damaged, if you are converting to a variable speed pump and want the circuit checked, or if you are adding a pool heat pump and need to know whether your panel can carry it.

Also call before a pool remodel. Redoing a deck is the cheapest possible moment to correct a bonding grid, and the most expensive moment to discover it later.

Name: How Many Circuits Does a Kitchen Need? An Arizona Remodel Wiring Guide
Post Body:
Here is the conversation we have in a lot of Valley kitchens. The cabinets are picked, the quartz is ordered, the contractor has a start date. Somebody asks what the electrical is going to run. And the honest answer is that it depends almost entirely on how many circuits are in that kitchen right now, which nobody has looked at yet.

A modern kitchen needs roughly seven or eight circuits. A kitchen built in Mesa or Chandler in 1988 often has three. That gap is the electrical budget, and it is worth understanding before the demo starts rather than after.

The Short Answer

For a typical all-electric kitchen, the list looks like this:

  • Two 20 amp small appliance circuits for the countertop receptacles. This is a minimum, not a target, and those circuits are not allowed to feed the lights or anything outside the countertop and dining areas.
  • One dedicated circuit for the refrigerator. Technically there is some flexibility here, but in practice every kitchen we wire gets its own fridge circuit, because you do not want a tripped breaker on a weekend away to cost you everything in the freezer.
  • One circuit for the dishwasher, which also needs ground fault protection.
  • One circuit for the garbage disposal. A disposal and dishwasher can share in limited cases, but separating them is cleaner and matches most appliance manufacturer instructions.
  • One dedicated circuit for a built-in microwave, whether it is over the range or in a cabinet.
  • One 240 volt circuit for the range or cooktop, usually 40 or 50 amps. A separate wall oven gets its own.
  • One lighting circuit for the ceiling cans, under-cabinet lighting, and any pendants.

Add a beverage fridge, a pot filler with a heated element nearby, a built-in coffee system, or a steam oven, and the count climbs from there.

What Older Valley Kitchens Actually Have

Go look in your panel. If your house went up in the 1970s or 1980s, the kitchen is commonly running on two small appliance circuits and a shared lighting circuit, and the microwave, the fridge, and sometimes the disposal are all riding on those same two.

That is why a lot of Valley homeowners live with the morning breaker dance: microwave plus toaster plus coffee maker equals a trip. People assume the breaker is weak. The breaker is fine. It is doing exactly what it is supposed to do on a circuit carrying three appliances that were never meant to share.

A remodel is the moment that gets fixed, because the walls are open and adding a circuit is a fraction of what it costs to fish one later.

Ground Fault and Arc Fault Protection

Two things have changed significantly over the last few code cycles and both will show up in your remodel.

GFCI protection has expanded a lot. It used to be countertop receptacles only. Recent code has pushed it well past that, into the dishwasher circuit and, in newer cycles, essentially every receptacle in the kitchen including the 240 volt ones. What your specific city enforces depends on which code cycle they are on, which is one of several reasons this is not a great place to work from a YouTube video. If you want the basics of how the device itself works, we wrote up how GFCI outlets work and how they are wired.

Arc fault protection applies to most of the rest. Arc fault breakers look for the signature of an arcing connection, which is the thing that actually starts electrical fires inside walls. In a remodel, new circuits generally get it.

The practical effect is that a modern kitchen panel has a lot more protective breakers in it than a 1985 panel did, and those breakers take space. Which leads to the part people do not expect.

The Panel Is Usually the Real Question

You cannot add five circuits to a panel that has no room and no capacity. On a lot of Valley remodels, the kitchen is the project and the panel is the actual cost.

Two separate issues:

Space. Physical slots for breakers. Tandems can sometimes buy a little room, but plenty of panels are already full of them.

Capacity. Whether the service itself can carry the new load. Going from a gas range to an induction cooktop, for instance, adds a serious 240 volt load that was not there before. So does adding a wall oven, and so does an EV charger somebody wants in the garage as part of the same project.

If the panel needs to come up, a like-for-like 200 amp replacement generally runs $5,200 to $6,500, or $6,400 to $8,750 when the meter base and panel are replaced together as an all-in-one. Our guide to the signs you need a panel upgrade covers what to look for, and the panels page has the details of the work.

Find this out in week one. The worst version of a kitchen remodel is the one where the cabinets are installed and then somebody discovers the induction cooktop has nowhere to land.

Outlet Placement, Islands, and the Details That Get Missed

Countertop receptacle spacing is governed so that no point along the counter is very far from a receptacle, which in practice means an outlet every few feet along any usable counter run, and any counter section a foot or wider gets one. It is a rule that exists so people stop running cords across sinks and cooktops.

Islands are the part that has genuinely moved across recent code cycles, and different Valley cities are on different cycles. The safe approach on an island is to plan for accessible power, get it designed with your electrician rather than assumed, and avoid the old trick of a receptacle mounted face up in the counter or tucked underneath where a cord can be pulled. Those have fallen out of favor for good reasons.

Other things that get missed constantly in remodels:

  • Under-cabinet lighting needs a switched circuit and a plan for where the driver and wiring hide. Decide before the backsplash goes on.
  • Recessed lighting layout is worth doing properly rather than putting cans on a grid. We covered the approach in our post on recessed lighting installation in Phoenix.
  • The range hood. A big hood needs its own circuit and a real duct run, not a recirculating filter, if you actually cook. Ductwork is not our trade, and it is the one part of a kitchen where we hand people to our sister company The Cooling Guy HVAC (Arizona ROC 364481) rather than guess.
  • Appliance garages and drawer microwaves need a receptacle located exactly where the cabinet maker expects it. Get the appliance specs before rough-in.

Going Gas to Induction

This comes up more every year, and it is straightforward as long as it is planned. An induction cooktop needs a dedicated 240 volt circuit, commonly 40 or 50 amps depending on the unit, run from the panel to the cooktop location.

The catch is that a gas kitchen was never wired for it. There is no existing 240 volt circuit behind that cabinet, so it is a new run plus a new breaker plus panel space, and it is exactly the sort of thing that is easy during demo and painful afterward. If induction is even on your list of maybes, run the circuit while the walls are open. An unused 240 volt circuit behind a cabinet is cheap insurance.

Timing: When the Electrician Should Be There

Kitchen remodels go well when the electrical happens in this order:

  1. Before design is locked. Panel evaluation and a load calculation. This tells you whether a panel upgrade is in the budget.
  2. After appliances are selected, before rough-in. Every circuit, receptacle location, and switch leg is decided off the actual appliance specs and the cabinet drawings.
  3. Rough-in with the walls open. New circuits, boxes, lighting, and any panel work.
  4. Trim out. Devices, fixtures, under-cabinet lighting, appliance connections, and testing.

The kitchens that get expensive are the ones where somebody tried to reuse existing circuits to save money and ended up with a brand new kitchen that still trips a breaker when the toaster and the air fryer run at the same time.
